title: Predict Walk-In Cooler Failures Via Refrigeration Techs
one_liner: White-label predictive monitoring that local commercial-refrigeration companies sell as a maintenance plan, so a failing compressor becomes a Tuesday service visit rather than a Saturday-night emergency.
customer: Independent commercial refrigeration and HVAC-R service companies with 5-50 techs, who pay roughly $8-12 per monitored compressor per month and resell at $25-40 inside a maintenance plan. The restaurant is the end payer. A later add-on is a spoilage-insurer premium discount.
problem: A walk-in dies on Saturday at 9pm. That means an emergency call at 2-3x the rate and $8-15k of protein and dairy in the dumpster, sometimes a closed kitchen. Temperature-probe alerts only fire after the box is already warm, so they are too late. The real early signals are in the power draw: rising duty cycle from dirty condenser coils, failing fan motors and capacitors, low charge, short-cycling, and defrost heater faults. Techs spend their weekends on emergencies and have almost no recurring revenue.
solution: Clip-on current-sensing hardware (roughly $25-40 bill of materials) with a cellular or Wi-Fi gateway on each compressor and condenser fan. A model compares duty cycle and amp draw against ambient kitchen temperature and defrost cycles to flag drift weeks before the box warms. It creates a scheduled work order in the contractor's dispatch system (for example ServiceTitan) with the likely fault and parts to bring. The contractor sells it as a 'Sunday-proof plan' and gets the white-label dashboard and monthly reports.
why_now: Cellular IoT and current sensors are very cheap. Field-service software has spread through small trades, so integrations are possible. Skilled refrigeration techs are scarce and contractors need each tech to cover more boxes. The HFC phasedown (AIM Act) is changing refrigerants and service complexity, pushing repair-versus-replace decisions. Power prices are climbing, so efficiency drift now costs owners visibly.
revenue_model: Recurring B2B2B: $8-12 per monitored compressor per month to the contractor, plus hardware at cost and a per-contractor platform fee. Later, add insurer partnerships that pay for verified spoilage-loss reductions.
non_obvious_insight: The real distribution channel for restaurant equipment tech is not SaaS marketing to owners. It is 'my guy': the one refrigeration tech who answers his phone. Owners trust him, he holds the keys and the relationship, and he hates 2am calls and lacks recurring revenue. Sell to Mike, not to me. The signal is also cheaper than probes: amp draw predicts failures that temperature only reveals when it is too late.
first_30_days: Instrument 10-15 compressors and condenser fans across my two locations and five friends' restaurants with off-the-shelf clamp sensors. Log data and record every failure. Sign 2-3 local refrigeration companies as design partners with a free 60-day pilot of 50 sensors. Use the first 'caught it before Saturday' event as the case study, then sell the plan to that contractor's other accounts.

title: Charged Battery Cylinders for Market Traders
one_liner: Deliver and swap standardised 2 kWh LFP packs daily to market traders, the way gas cylinders are sold.
customer: Market traders, salons, food vendors and phone-charging kiosks in Lagos, Kano, Nairobi and Accra.
problem: These businesses run petrol and diesel generators or lose sales in outages, and cannot afford upfront batteries even as Africa imports more battery dollars than panels.
solution: Rugged handled LFP packs, solar-charged at rooftop depots and swapped daily by motorcycle couriers on a per-swap subscription. The wedge is 200 vendors around one market served from a depot with about 60 packs.
why_now: LFP cell prices are low, the fuel-price shock hurts generator users, and distributed solar is already scaling faster than utility supply.
revenue_model: $0.80-1.50 per swap, with 30-40% gross margin at about 70% pack utilisation.
non_obvious_insight: Small traders buy energy the way they buy gas, in small frequent delivered units. A swap network amortises battery cost across many users and removes the upfront barrier.
first_30_days: Build 30 packs and run swaps for 20 vendors at one market to measure utilisation and pack cycle life.

title: Retreat Options for Eroding Oceanfront Homes
one_liner: An annual retainer that reserves a house-mover and demolition slot and triggers automatically when satellite-measured setback hits a preset distance.
customer: Owners of oceanfront and bluff homes on the Outer Banks and Cape Hatteras, Great Lakes bluffs, Maine and Nantucket, and California bluffs. Secondary buyers are lenders, county governments and the National Park Service.
problem: 32 oceanfront houses have collapsed along Cape Hatteras National Seashore since 2020, four in one February 2026 weekend. Owners bear removal costs of roughly $120K to demolish or $100K-$200K to move. NFIP pays nothing pre-collapse, and contractor capacity is overwhelmed exactly when it is needed. NFIP pre-collapse coverage has been proposed but not enacted.
solution: Pooled owners pay a retainer for two things. First, monthly satellite measurement of foundation-to-scarp or vegetation-line distance from 30-50 cm imagery, with pre-storm tasking, and archive imagery to compute each home's 5-10 year retreat rate. Second, pre-negotiated capacity with movers and demolition contractors. Preset thresholds automatically mobilise the contractor and deliver a dated evidence file. That file doubles as claim documentation if NFIP pre-collapse legislation passes and gives lenders and counties a trusted trigger. Structured as a service and capacity contract rather than insurance.
why_now: FEMA's lack of any pre-collapse option is national news in September 2026 (NPR), and the Outer Banks lost 20 Buxton houses in a year. Pre-collapse coverage legislation is pending. Cheap oversupplied commercial imagery makes pooled tasking affordable (one 25 km2 pass covers about 10 km of coast and hundreds of homes).
revenue_model: $1,800/yr retainer per home. An 8-10% referral fee on move or demolition jobs. County and NPS triage contracts. Lender monitoring feeds at $10-20 per loan per month.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce resource is neither money nor measurement but contractor capacity at the moment of crisis. An option on that capacity, triggered by a measurement all parties trust, is a new kind of asset. Neighbours pooling their tasking makes the satellite cost trivial per home.
first_30_days: Sign 2 Outer Banks or Great Lakes house-movers and demolition firms to retainer terms. Pull archive imagery to compute 5-year retreat rates for about 200 threatened homes, then approach owner associations in Buxton and Rodanthe with each home's own curve. Enrol 10 homes at $1,200 founder pricing.

title: Instant Will-Serve Letters From Hydraulic Models
one_liner: Turn a utility's calibrated hydraulic model into a self-serve 'can you serve this address?' oracle that issues fire-flow and will-serve determinations in 48 hours instead of 4 weeks. It starts with developers and sprinkler designers and grows into a water-readiness index for data center and fab site selectors.
customer: Small and mid-size water utilities and the consulting engineering firms that maintain their models are the sellers. The payers are housing developers and fire sprinkler design firms ($250-2,000 per request), then data center, fab and beverage-plant site selection teams ($20-100k per year for the readiness data).
problem: Every subdivision, sprinkler design and industrial hookup needs a will-serve or fire-flow letter. Utilities own a calibrated hydraulic model (WaterGEMS, InfoWater, EPANET), but one or two engineers, or an outside consultant billing $2-8k per run, can operate it. Requests queue for weeks and stall housing and economic development. Worse, the answer 'we have plenty of water' is meaningless. The binding limits are max-day and peak-hour pressure in one pressure zone, fire reserve storage, tank turnover and water age, and the wastewater plant's discharge limits. Big buyers don't know that, and many utilities can't answer within the time a site-selection process allows.
solution: Ingest the utility's model file (.inp or vendor formats) and pre-compute a grid of scenarios. For each node and pressure zone, calculate available fire flow at a 20 psi residual, the maximum added demand before minimum-pressure or velocity limits break, and the effect on tank cycling and water age. Wrap it in a web form and API: enter address, demand, fire-flow requirement, and get a preliminary letter with the utility's letterhead, assumptions and limits. Exceptions go to the utility's licensed engineer for review and stamp. Utilities set the fee and keep most of it. The large-load layer adds wastewater and pretreatment limits, reclaimed-water availability, drought stage and water-rights status. It is published as a 'water hookup readiness' score by utility, like the power-availability maps that data center developers already buy.
why_now: The data center build-out has made water availability a headline and a local permitting fight, and site selection teams already buy power-availability intelligence but have no water equivalent. Housing permitting reform is speeding the approvals that come before utility review, which makes the utility review the bottleneck. Open-source tooling (EPANET and Sandia's WNTR) plus LLM agents that can read model files and draft letters make productizing this feasible for a small team. Many utilities finished models under recent risk-and-resilience assessments and master plans, so the models exist and are unused.
revenue_model: Utility SaaS of $15-40k per year, or free in exchange for a revenue share on developer fees. Per-request fees of $250-2,000 paid by developers, with the utility keeping 50-70%. Data subscriptions of $20-100k per year to site selectors, land brokers and hyperscaler real-estate teams. A consulting-firm channel where the engineering firm resells to its 10-30 utility clients.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce resource is not water. It is the one person who is allowed to run the model. The calibrated model is the most valuable unused asset a utility owns, and the answer developers want is hydraulic (peak-day and fire-flow at one node), not a volume in an annual water permit.
first_30_days: Approach one consulting engineering firm that maintains models for 10 or more small utilities and pitch productizing its most repeated task. Build a thin front end on WNTR or EPANET and offer one utility a free pilot: a public fire-flow map plus a letter template. Run the first 20 requests semi-manually, with the engineer generating and signing outputs in the background. Charge local sprinkler design firms $250 per fire-flow letter. Use the results to show turnaround times to two more utilities and to start a data-center-readiness prototype for one region.

title: Evacuation Lift Registry Ending Double-Booked Buses
one_liner: A neutral county-level registry that guarantees each ambulance, wheelchair van and bus seat is promised to only one nursing home per storm, paid for by facilities and by carriers who finally get standby retainers.
customer: Paying: multi-site nursing home and assisted-living operators (SaaS per facility) and ambulance/NEMT/charter-bus operators (platform fee on standby retainers). Sponsoring: county emergency managers and healthcare coalitions using preparedness grants.
problem: The CMS emergency preparedness rule makes every facility hold transportation agreements, but no one checks whether the same 40 wheelchair vans and ambulances are 'contracted' by 300 facilities. GAO and post-Katrina research found carriers holding contracts with many facilities in one community, which works for a single-building evacuation and collapses when a whole county goes at once. Facilities learn at H-48 that their contract is one of a dozen identical promises. Carriers do not honor a promise they were never paid to hold.
solution: Borrow the military's lift-allocation discipline, where an asset can appear on the movement plan only once. Facilities reserve capacity by resident mix (ambulatory, wheelchair, stretcher, oxygen or vent-dependent), not by 'beds'. The registry totals promised demand against real vehicle capacity by county and flags oversubscription weeks before the season, then matches the gap to out-of-region carriers on paid standby. At activation it issues a departure-window movement table so convoys do not collide, plus manifest and accountability packets for each facility. Before activation it stores only aggregate counts by acuity, not PHI, which keeps HIPAA scope small.
why_now: The President's FEMA Review Council final report (May 7, 2026) recommends disaster response be 'locally executed, state managed, federally supported'. Counties and healthcare coalitions are inheriting logistics they never staffed, with less federal backfill. It is peak hurricane season, and post-acute care closures and consolidation are concentrating residents into fewer, larger buildings.
revenue_model: $150-400 per facility per month. Carriers pay 8-12% on standby retainers the platform brokers, which they never received before. Optional county or coalition license of $25-100k a year, funded by ASPR HPP or EMPG grants. Later, add-ons for dialysis centers, group homes and inpatient rehab.
non_obvious_insight: Vehicles are not the shortage. Unique promises are. Every evacuation failure post-mortem says 'not enough buses', but the fleet often exists and is simply committed many times over. Military movement planners never let one lift asset appear twice on a time-phased deployment plan, while civilian planners have nobody whose job is to check. Loading time is also the hidden constraint: a stretcher resident takes about 20 minutes to load, so acuity mix, not headcount, determines how many vehicles you need.
first_30_days: Pick one storm-prone county cluster (Tampa Bay, coastal Carolinas or Louisiana parishes). Ask 10 facilities to share their transport MOUs, which they must keep on file for CMS surveys anyway. Build the overlap heat map by hand in a spreadsheet, for example 'nine of your ten facilities are promised the same carrier'. Take it to the county emergency manager and the healthcare coalition coordinator. Convert 3-5 facilities to a paid pilot at about $200 a month and sign 2 carriers to retainer contracts. Build the product as Airtable plus a simple web form before writing real software.

title: Real Gross Margin Diligence for AI Startups
one_liner: Quality-of-earnings for agent companies: restate COGS at unsubsidized token prices, retry waste and expiring credits so investors see true unit economics.
customer: Growth-equity, PE and VC diligence teams and corporate M&A groups acquiring AI-native companies ($20M-$500M deals), and startups preparing a raise.
problem: Reported AI gross margins are flattered by free cloud and model credits, introductory rates and uncosted retries. Practitioners say diligence restates credits at renewal prices, and AI-native margins run around 50-60% versus 75-85% for classic SaaS. Agentic tasks use 5-30x more tokens, so cohort economics move fast. M&A is heating up (Okta bought Permiso for about $200M in July 2026, and Palo Alto bought Portkey and Koi). Traditional QoE firms lack telemetry fluency.
solution: Read-only connectors to billing exports, gateways, cloud invoices and product analytics. Produce cohort-level unsubsidized COGS per seat or outcome, sensitivity to price cuts and model swaps, tokens per customer growth, cost of failed runs and retries, and scaling curves. Five-day turnaround report, plus quarterly monitoring for fund portfolios.
why_now: An AI M&A wave and investors pricing trajectory over current margin. Credit-inflated margins matter more as promotional pricing expires, and 73% of enterprises overran AI budgets.
revenue_model: $15-$40k per diligence engagement and $3-$8k/month portfolio monitoring subscriptions for funds.
non_obvious_insight: The margin story is hidden in gateway and billing logs, not the general ledger. Buyers pay a premium to avoid overpaying for subsidized revenue, and every engagement builds a private benchmark of credit-adjusted margins.
first_30_days: Write the data-request list and report template. Pitch 20 growth-stage funds and deal associates, deliver 2 discounted diligence reports, and publish an anonymized credit-adjusted gross margin benchmark to generate inbound.

title: Data Act Unlock for Hotel Connected Equipment
one_liner: Use the EU Data Act's user-access rights to pull hotels' own data out of locked vendor clouds (HVAC, locks, laundry, elevators) into an energy and maintenance ledger that third-party service firms can plug into.
customer: EU independent hotel groups and management companies with 5-50 properties, plus independent HVAC, elevator and kitchen-equipment service firms and energy-optimization vendors that want the data.
problem: After the 2026 Hormuz energy shock, hotel energy costs have been repriced sharply. The data from a hotel's connected thermostats, HVAC, locks, laundry and elevators is trapped in manufacturers' clouds, resold as premium dashboards or API fees. A mixed-brand group cannot build a unified view, and independent maintenance firms cannot diagnose without OEM tools.
solution: Since Sep 2025 the Data Act has let users demand the data generated by connected products and have it shared with a third party they choose (free to the user, on my reading, so verify). New products must offer access by design from 12 Sep 2026. The service is a request desk (letter templates, deadline tracking per OEM, escalation to the national authority) plus connectors that load the data into a property energy and asset ledger, with consent logs for designated recipients.
why_now: The Sep 2026 design-by-default date has just passed and vendors are unprepared, so early requests set the precedents. Energy-cost pain makes the hotel side motivated. The brief also shows small hardware makers scrambling with Data Act and CRA duties, so vendors are stretched.
revenue_model: About EUR 200 per property per month, 10-15% of verified energy savings, and onboarding fees paid by service firms and optimizers who become designated recipients.
non_obvious_insight: Hotels are among the largest accidental 'users' under the Data Act, with dozens of connected products per building, and nobody has told them. The law turns vendor lock-in into a right, the way GDPR created a market for data-subject-request services.
first_30_days: Sign one 10-property group for a flat EUR 1,500 'Data Act audit plus first requests'. Inventory its connected assets, send about 20 access requests across 5 OEMs, and document responses and escalations. Then sell the same audit to 4 more groups and pitch one independent service firm as a designated recipient.

title: Flat-Fee Guarantee Against Runaway Agent Bills
one_liner: Pay a few percent on top of model spend and the guarantee absorbs any overnight blowout above a hard multiple of baseline, enforced by an inline kill switch.
customer: AI-native startups and agencies spending $5k-$200k per month on model and tool calls (seed to Series B), including dev shops deploying agents for clients.
problem: Retry loops turn $0.40 tasks into $40, and five-figure overnight bills are reported. Blended token prices fell about 67% in a year but agentic workflows burn 5-30x more tokens, and 73% of enterprises overran AI budgets. The market sells dashboards and caps. Nobody sells a promise, and founders and their investors want the tail risk gone.
solution: A drop-in proxy (change one base URL) that sees all model and tool traffic and learns a rolling baseline per agent and workflow. The guarantee covers spend above a set multiple of baseline in a rolling window (for example 4x over 6 hours), up to a cap, paid as cash or credits. The proxy enforces circuit breakers so maximum loss is bounded, which makes underwriting tractable. Coverage applies only where default breaker policies were accepted, which controls moral hazard.
why_now: TechCrunch was covering the scramble over runaway AI costs by June 2026. Gateways are being absorbed into security suites (Palo Alto bought Portkey), and dozens of cap-and-alert tools have commoditized enforcement without offering a guarantee.
revenue_model: 3-6% premium on metered spend plus a gateway subscription, with parametric or MGA reinsurance for large limits.
non_obvious_insight: Whoever owns the kill switch can price the tail. A capped, enforced exposure is a parametric insurance product, not an open-ended liability. Buyers are paying for certainty, and the tooling is only how you deliver it.
first_30_days: Ship an OpenAI- and Anthropic-compatible proxy with breakers. Sign 10 startups to a beta guarantee capped at about $2k per incident, backed by a roughly $20k reserve. Price at about 4% of spend and log every incident. Talk to two parametric or MGA capacity providers.

title: Buy the Orphaned License of Dead Models
one_liner: Acquire or secure exclusive commercial-licensing rights to hugely downloaded open models and tools whose company died, then sell clean, warranted commercial licenses plus a public orphan-license registry.
customer: Startups and mid-size companies shipping voice features (dubbing, audiobooks, IVR, game NPC voices, accessibility) on top of XTTS-class models, and the procurement or legal teams of their enterprise buyers who now ask for model-license provenance.
problem: Coqui XTTS-v2 is still pulled about 6.75M times a month under a non-commercial license (CPML), but Coqui shut down in Dec 2023. Commercial licensing was 'available upon inquiry' from a company that no longer exists, so builders either violate the license, ship legal risk to customers, or rip out the best multilingual voice-cloning model. GitHub threads asking about commercial use or the license after shutdown were closed 'wontfix'.
solution: Phase 1: trace the rights chain (Coqui Inc., founders, assignees, any bankruptcy or dissolution filings) and option an exclusive commercial-licensing agency deal or outright IP purchase, which should be cheap because the seller is a dead startup. Phase 2: sell per-product annual commercial licenses ($2k-$25k) with a written rights-chain warranty and an audit letter that customers can hand to enterprise procurement. Phase 3: publish an Orphan Model Registry (model, steward status, license, who can grant commercial rights) as a free lead-gen asset and a paid API for AI-governance tools. Fallback if the rights-holder refuses: sell a fixed-price license-risk audit and a swap-to-permissive-model migration (Apache/MIT TTS) with regression tests.
why_now: Enterprise AI-governance questionnaires in 2026 ask for model and data provenance. The $1.5B Anthropic authors settlement (2025) and the Authors Guild v. OpenAI/Microsoft unsealed briefs (HN front page 2026-09-27, 626 points) made license hygiene a board-level topic. Open voice tools are exploding: VoiceStudio hit 43.9k stars, +27k in one month, and its README warns each bundled model has its own license to review before commercial use.
revenue_model: Annual per-product licenses ($2k-$25k), enterprise-wide licenses, audit and migration fees ($3k-$8k fixed price), registry API subscription ($200-$1k a month).
non_obvious_insight: Demand is already proven and supply is literally zero: nobody can sell a commercial license because the seller is dead, so dead-startup IP is the scarcest cheap asset in open AI. Evidence: XTTS-v2 shows 6,752,613 downloads last month under CPML (https://huggingface.co/coqui/XTTS-v2). Coqui repo issues on commercial use, license after shutdown and 'Move to MIT' are closed wontfix (https://github.com/coqui-ai/TTS/issues?q=commercial+license+is%3Aissue). Issue #4022, opened nearly a year after shutdown, says the community is confused about 'commercial use and fine-tuning' (https://github.com/coqui-ai/TTS/issues/4022). HN, Nov 2023: XTTS stays non-commercial with commercial licensing 'upon inquiry'. VoiceStudio's AGPL repo warns model licenses vary (https://github.com/debpalash/VoiceStudio).
first_30_days: Days 1-7: pull Delaware and other corporate records for Coqui Inc., message the founders and former staff, and draft a one-page option agreement (small cash plus revenue share). Days 1-10: build the registry from 50 popular non-commercial or orphaned models on Hugging Face. Days 10-30: email companies that opened XTTS licensing issues and companies whose products visibly use XTTS (from public GitHub dependency graphs) with a $3k risk audit, and aim for 3-5 paid audits. If the rights option lands, convert those audits into licenses.

title: Pharma Load Attribution for EU Producer-Pays Wastewater
one_liner: A neutral, audit-grade dataset showing which drugs from which producers, in which aging catchments and care homes, create the micropollutant load that EU pharma companies must now pay at least 80% of treatment for.
customer: National extended-producer-responsibility scheme operators and pharma/cosmetics trade bodies. Regional water boards and utilities deciding which large plants get quaternary treatment first also buy. Pricing is EUR 25-80k per study and EUR 100-250k a year for licenses.
problem: The recast Urban Wastewater Directive makes pharma and cosmetics producers fund at least 80% of quaternary treatment. The payment scheme is due by end-2028, and 20% of large plants must be upgraded by 2033. Annual cost estimates differ about 10x (EC EUR 1.2B, JRC EUR 1.56B, EurEau EUR 3.6-11.2B, Spain alone EUR 24.5B), and nobody owns the attribution of kilograms of active ingredient to payers. Older adults, care homes and hospitals are the concentrated source of medication residues, and Europe's 80+ cohort is its fastest-growing.
solution: A catchment-level model combining national dispensing statistics by age band, care-home and hospital bed registers, excretion and plant-removal rates, and receiving-water flow. It is validated by composite sampling at a handful of plants. It outputs load by active ingredient by plant, mapped to marketing-authorization-holder market shares for an allocation formula. A 'source-control screen' flags plants where pretreatment at a large care home or hospital removes more load per euro than plant-scale ozone or activated carbon, as a candidate for levy credits. The methodology is published so the scheme operator can defend it.
why_now: The directive is in transposition and the scheme design is being fought over now. The 10x cost disagreement means both utilities and producers need defensible numbers before 2028. European aging keeps raising per-capita medication load.
revenue_model: Per-study fees of EUR 25-80k for water boards. Annual licenses of EUR 100-250k to national scheme operators and industry associations for the allocation engine and yearly re-runs. Later, consulting on care-home source-control projects.
non_obvious_insight: The cost fight will be won by whoever supplies a referee-grade attribution dataset. The best predictor of load is not at the pipe but at the pillbox: age-structured dispensing and care-home density explain most of it. Demographics is the missing variable in water-quality economics, and neither water engineers nor pharma-market analysts hold both halves.
first_30_days: Start with the Netherlands and Germany, where open national dispensing statistics exist (for example the Dutch GIP databank). Model 5 mid-size catchments. Cold-pitch two regional water boards and one pharma producer association with the one-page result. Aim to close paid pilots at EUR 15-25k.

title: Court-Ready Estate Accounting from Bank Statements
one_liner: Upload the statements and get the court's accounting format back, so small probate firms stop losing money on the ledger.
customer: Solo and small estate and trust law firms, CPAs acting as fiduciaries, professional fiduciaries, and small trust desks at community banks.
problem: Inventories, receipts-and-disbursements accountings and trust accountings to beneficiaries take 10-30+ hours per estate. Each state and county wants a different format. Small firms bill flat fees or lose money, and errors cause objections and surcharges.
solution: Upload bank and brokerage statements (PDF or CSV). The system categorizes transactions into principal and income, ties to date-of-death balances, flags unusual disbursements, and exports state-format accountings. Start with California plus one more high-volume state (New York or Pennsylvania). A reviewer trail records every override. Later add fiduciary 1041 data and distribution schedules.
why_now: LLM document extraction only recently became reliable on messy statements. Revocable-trust use has grown with online will and trust providers, so more successor trustees face accounting duties.
revenue_model: $149-$399 per accounting or $199-$499/month per firm, with enterprise pricing for banks.
non_obvious_insight: The bottleneck in probate isn't drafting, it's the ledger, and the ledger is what judges and beneficiaries inspect. Whoever owns the estate ledger owns the workflow and the data for tax, inventory and distributions.
first_30_days: Pick California. Recruit 10 small firms through bar section lists. Process 20 accountings manually for $199 each while capturing the county format rules. Publish a sample output for lead generation.

title: Peptide Assurance Mark for Clinics and Processors
one_liner: Independent lot testing and supplier audit with a QR-verifiable mark that lets peptide sellers pass payment-processor and insurer underwriting.
customer: 503A compounding pharmacies, peptide and longevity clinic chains, and the payment processors and insurers who need evidence to underwrite them.
problem: HHS moved ~14 of 19 Category 2 peptides (BPC-157, TB-500, GHK-Cu and others) back toward compoundable in Feb 2026, and an FDA panel backed BPC-157 and KPV on Jul 23. Clinics are multiplying, but Stripe and card networks exclude the category and Forbes (Jun 30, 2026) called it a '$1 billion industry banks won't touch'. Losing a merchant account kills sellers faster than FDA action.
solution: ISO 17025 lab partners test identity, purity, endotoxin, sterility and potency per lot. Supplier and chain-of-custody audits feed a public registry and QR verification that processors, insurers and state boards can accept, with annual certification and monitoring.
why_now: The legal window opened in 2026 with no infrastructure. Purity is uneven, and processors need third-party evidence to underwrite certified merchants.
revenue_model: $250-600 per lot test, $5-15k/year certification, and processor referral fees for certified merchants.
non_obvious_insight: The bottleneck is payments and insurance, not FDA. A credible independent mark is the key that unlocks mainstream merchant accounts, so processors are the hidden buyer.
first_30_days: Contract an accredited lab and run a blind-purchase audit of 30 popular BPC-157 and GHK-Cu products, published as a report. Sell $500 audits to 10 clinics and approach two high-risk processors about fast-tracking certified merchants.

title: Brewery Tank-Time for Fermentation Startups
one_liner: Rent the empty fermenters of struggling craft breweries to early-stage fermentation companies that cannot get pilot-scale capacity, with standard SOPs and insurance.
customer: Buyers: seed-to-Series-A companies making probiotics and postbiotics, lactic-acid-bacteria and yeast-based ingredients, cultured foods, kombucha-adjacent drinks and biocontrol products that need 1 to 30 kL runs. Sellers: craft breweries, cideries and distilleries with idle tanks.
problem: Pilot-scale food-grade fermentation capacity is scarce and expensive for startups. Meanwhile the Brewers Association says breweries used only about 55% of capacity in 2024, there were 481 closures against 300 openings in 2025, and US craft breweries fell to 9,344 by June 2026. Neither side knows how to contract safely, and food-safety, TTB and insurance issues block informal deals.
solution: A marketplace with a standardized brewery-as-CDMO package: BSL-1 organism screening, cleaning and changeover SOPs, food-facility registration checks, TTB premises guidance, a template contract and insurer-backed coverage. A rentable clip-on aeration and dissolved-oxygen kit extends tanks to low-aeration aerobic processes. Startups book tank-days and downstream time (centrifuge, filtration, cold room).
why_now: Craft brewing is in a third year of decline, with real estate and tank capacity stranded. Startup funding is tight, so cheap pilot capacity matters. Sensors and remote fermentation monitoring make third-party oversight feasible.
revenue_model: Startups pay $300 to $900 per tank-day; the brewery keeps about 80%, the platform takes 15% to 20%. Fees for SOP set-up, kit rental and insurance referral.
non_obvious_insight: Tanks are not the scarce input; validated protocols and biosafety trust are. Most brewery fermenters are unstirred and anaerobic, so the honest wedge is anaerobic and low-aeration products, with an aeration retrofit unlocking more later. A platform that standardizes the SOP and contract becomes the default channel.
first_30_days: Recruit 8 breweries within a few hours of Boston, the Bay Area or Denver that have idle 10-to-30-barrel fermenters. Work with a food-safety consultant to write a one-organism SOP. Approach 25 fermentation startups and run 3 paid pilot batches at $2k to $5k each.

title: Exosuit-as-a-Service Paid by Workers' Comp Carriers
one_liner: Rentable powered back-and-hip assist suits for home-care aides and nursing assistants, with usage data that earns workers' comp premium credits.
customer: Home-care agencies and nursing-home operators with high workers' comp experience mods, workers' comp carriers and MGAs with loss-control budgets, and PEOs.
problem: Aides and nursing assistants have some of the highest musculoskeletal injury rates, and a claim costs tens of thousands. Agencies can't install ceiling lifts in clients' homes, and with 77-80% turnover, injuries drive both cost and churn.
solution: Rent-by-month lightweight powered assist suits with sizing, training and warranty. Onboard sensors count bends and lifts to build injury-risk analytics for the carrier, who credits premiums. Start with clients who need transfers, and use it as a retention perk.
why_now: Consumer-priced powered exosuits appeared in 2025-26, and workforce scarcity makes worker safety and retention perks valuable. Comp carriers are actively looking for loss-control programs in a squeezed home-health margin environment.
revenue_model: $60-100 per suit per month paid by the agency or shared with the carrier, performance rebates, and an analytics subscription.
non_obvious_insight: Sell to the party that pays for injuries (the carrier), not the aide, and let data turn a gadget into a premium negotiation. Lab claims of strain reduction still need real-world proof, which the pilot supplies.
first_30_days: Lease 30 suits from an OEM, find two agencies and a regional comp carrier, and run a 90-day trial measuring injuries, lost workdays and turnover.

title: Wildfire Evacuation Autopilot for Campsites and Hotels
one_liner: Satellite fire-spread alerts plus pre-contracted buses, routes and multilingual guest messaging turn every tourist lodging in fire country into an evacuation node.
customer: Campsites, holiday parks and hotels in fire-prone Mediterranean regions (France's Aude, Var and Gironde, Catalonia, Greece, Portugal, Croatia), plus regional tourism boards and insurers.
problem: Summer wildfires now force sudden evacuations of thousands of tourists who have no local knowledge, often no cars and no shared language. Duty of care sits with small operators holding paper plans they have never drilled, while insurers tighten terms.
solution: A site-specific evacuation plan with two routes and a refuge, ingestion of hourly fire detections (NASA FIRMS, Copernicus EFFIS and commercial satellite feeds), wind-aware fire arrival estimates per site, and automatic guest alerts by WhatsApp or SMS in the guest's language using check-in data. It includes a staff checklist and drills, and standby contracts with local coach operators.
why_now: Higher-frequency satellite fire detection arrived with early-2025 launches such as FireSat, and wildfire seasons in 2025 were severe across Southern Europe. Insurers and regulators are pressing small operators.
revenue_model: EUR 300-1,200 per site per year, margin on coach standby retainers, insurer premium-discount share and regional government contracts.
non_obvious_insight: Tourist lodging is the largest concentration of people in fire zones with no local knowledge, no vehicles and no common language, and the legal duty sits with operators who cannot afford risk consultants.
first_30_days: Recruit 25 campsites in Aude, Hérault, Var and Gironde through the camping federation. Deliver a plan PDF and WhatsApp alerts at EUR 390 per year, run one drill and pitch two insurers with results.

title: Permit Concierge for Rare-Plant and Reptile Sellers
one_liner: A checkout-integrated paperwork and permit service that lets hobby breeders of orchids, aroids, cacti, tarantulas and reptiles legally fill foreign orders instead of pushing buyers to the gray market.
customer: Independent rare-plant sellers (Instagram, Etsy, Facebook groups), hobby reptile/amphibian/invertebrate breeders, and small orchid/succulent nurseries doing $3k+/month that keep turning away foreign orders. Expo organizers and hobby societies (aroid, orchid, reptile expos) are a channel.
problem: All orchids and cacti, plus many other hobby species, are CITES-listed. Cross-border shipments need phytosanitary certificates, CITES export/import permits (which vary by country and by whether specimens are artificially propagated), US Lacey Act declarations, and import-inspection compliance on the EU/UK side. CITES CoP20 (Nov-Dec 2025) added listings that phase in during 2026 (verify). The paperwork is per-shipment, per-country and slow, so honest sellers refuse foreign orders, buyers turn to smugglers, and a small mistake means seizure or fines.
solution: A per-shipment service. The seller enters species and origin (propagated or wild). The system determines required documents by destination (CITES appendix and exemptions, phytosanitary certificate, carrier acceptance rules), pre-fills forms, books inspections and generates paperwork packets. It maintains a 'propagation record book' for each seller (dated photos, invoices, mother-plant records) to evidence the artificially-propagated exemption. A Shopify/Etsy plug-in quotes or blocks foreign orders with the permit fee included. A licensed customs broker/permit expeditor is the operating partner, and a wildlife-law attorney handles edge cases.
why_now: New CITES listings from CoP20 phase in through 2026 (verify). Post-Brexit UK rules and the EU Plant Health Regulation (fully applicable since Dec 2019) mean plant parcels need phytosanitary certificates, and platform and law-enforcement attention to online wildlife trade keeps rising. Rare-plant and exotic-pet hobby demand stayed high after 2020, so more sellers are hitting the cliff.
revenue_model: $89-349 per shipment. $39/month pro plan that includes the propagation record book and checkout plug-in. Referral fees from carriers/brokers. Sponsored compliance desks at hobby expos.
non_obvious_insight: Enforcement targets traffickers, but the practical legal cliff is for honest small sellers. The exemption for artificially propagated specimens means documentation of propagation is the real product: a provenance book. A seller with a clean book can charge a premium and reach EU/UK buyers competitors cannot, and a 'permit-verified' badge becomes a moat as platforms tighten.
first_30_days: Pick one lane, either CITES-listed succulents/orchids US-to-EU/UK or captive-bred reptiles. Partner with an experienced permit expeditor. Publish a free 'what paperwork does my plant need' checker to collect leads. Sign 10 sellers with pending foreign orders and process 30 shipments at about $150 each. Use the results to build templates and the propagation-book format.

title: Contingency Audit of Unbilled Plumbing Materials
one_liner: Reconcile a trade shop's supply-house invoices against its customer invoices and catch both parts that were bought but never billed and quiet supplier price drift, paid a percentage of what gets recovered.
customer: Plumbing, HVAC and electrical shops doing $1.5-15M in revenue with 5-40 techs, running ServiceTitan, Housecall Pro or Jobber plus QuickBooks, buying on account from Ferguson, Hajoca, Winsupply or a local supply house.
problem: Shops lose margin in two places nobody watches. First, parts go out on a supply-house ticket with a job name, or come off the truck stock, and never make it onto the customer invoice. Techs charge the labor from the flat-rate book and forget the $6 valve, the wax ring, the supply lines, the $40 of fittings. In the shops I know, when the office finally reconciles a quarter it is typically a few percent of revenue. Second, supply houses price off list with a contractor multiplier, and list prices have moved several times since the Section 232 copper, steel and aluminum tariffs (50%, working through a long manufacturer-to-contractor lag). Surcharges appear, job-quoted prices are not honored, returns credits are never issued, and no owner has time to read 40 invoices a week.
solution: Shops set up an email forwarding rule for supply-house invoices and statements and give us read access to their field-service software export. An LLM-based line-item parser ties supply-house lines to jobs and POs, then produces a weekly leak list for the office manager: (1) purchased-not-billed by job, (2) price versus the shop's own multiplier and versus the same SKU 30 days ago, (3) unclaimed return credits, (4) pricebook items where cost has risen past the target markup, with a repricing file ready to import. Later add a benchmark ('you pay 9% more than shops your size for PEX-A fittings') built from pooled anonymized invoices, which is the moat.
why_now: Tariff-driven price volatility means flat-rate pricebooks are stale within a quarter, and owners know it. Invoice parsing with LLMs went from a custom-ML project to an afternoon. Field-service platforms expose APIs and exports. The trades are also ahead of everyone else in adopting software but behind in auditing it, so there is no incumbent audit product.
revenue_model: Contingency fee of 25% of recovered and newly captured revenue for the first 12 months (no recovery, no fee), converting to a $199-499 per month subscription for continuous monitoring plus the pricing benchmark. Data licensing of the pooled price index to distributors and manufacturers later.
non_obvious_insight: Owners obsess over lead cost and tech hiring while the highest-ROI dollar is sitting in the shoebox of paid invoices. Everything a tech installs was bought on a ticket with a job name on it, so the truth is already in two systems that have never been compared. This is the freight-audit and telecom-audit model, and no one has brought it to the trades because the people who feel the pain are too busy running trucks to build it.
first_30_days: Offer a free 90-day audit to 10 shop owners from a peer group (a PHCC chapter, Nexstar or Service Roundtable style mastermind). Have them forward statements and give a one-time export. Turn each audit around in 48 hours with a single 'found money' number and a list of specific invoices. Convert the shops with the largest number to the contingency contract. A spreadsheet plus an LLM parsing script is enough for the first ten.

title: Open-Banking Rails for EU Connected Products
one_liner: A consent-and-access hub that lets manufacturers meet the EU Data Act's access-by-design duty and lets owners route product data to repairers, insurers and energy optimizers through one integration.
customer: Two sides. Forced buyers are manufacturers, importers and white-labelers of connected products sold in the EU (e-bikes, heat pumps, wallboxes, appliances, machinery, agricultural kit, wearables), paying per product family per year. The network side is independent repair chains, insurers, energy retailers, lenders and fleet managers paying per authorized device pull.
problem: Since 12 Sept 2026, connected products newly placed on the EU market must give users free, structured, machine-readable access to their data and share it with third parties on request. Most SME makers and importers have cloud endpoints never designed for this: no consent flow, no standard API, no logging, no trade-secret safeguards, no pre-sale disclosures. Third parties who want the data face hundreds of separate negotiations.
solution: A hosted 'Data Act portal' for the manufacturer covering ownership binding (QR or serial on the product), machine-readable export, consent to share with a named third party, trade-secret safeguards, access logs, a dispute workflow and the Art. 3(2) pre-contract disclosure templates. A normalized schema catalog per product category (for example 'heat pump v1') means third parties integrate once. We sell it first as a 90-day compliance kit, then monetize the network.
why_now: The access-by-design duty took effect 12 Sept 2026 and law-firm alerts show many makers unfinished. From 12 Jan 2027 cloud switching fees vanish, which makes data mobility a political priority. The regulation mandates giving data but says nothing about how anyone receives it.
revenue_model: Compliance SaaS at roughly EUR 300-3,000/month per product family. Network fees of EUR 0.02-0.50 per device per month from third-party consumers of the data. An optional certification badge for makers.
non_obvious_insight: The Data Act is open banking for machines, but with no PSD2-style standardization mandate: it creates a duty to give data with no way to receive it. Whoever standardizes the receiving side becomes the Plaid of physical products. The manufacturers, who are forced buyers today, pay for the network build.
first_30_days: Pick one fragmented vertical (e-bikes, or heat pumps and wallboxes). Publish a free 'is my product in scope' checker and a readiness checklist to generate leads. Sign 5 SME makers or importers to EUR 2k pilots that deliver a working access endpoint. Pitch two independent repair, insurance or energy firms as first consumers on the receiving side.

title: Aid-in-Dying Program-in-a-Box for Hospices
one_liner: Sell newly-legal states' hospices and health systems the policies, forms, trained consulting-clinician panel and logistics they need to participate in medical aid in dying.
customer: Independent hospices, palliative practices and non-religious health systems in Illinois and New York, then Massachusetts and Pennsylvania if they pass. The buyer is the medical director or administrator.
problem: Legalization creates a right on paper. The bottleneck is willing, trained clinicians (attending plus consulting physician, and mental-health evaluation where required), statutory documentation, waiting periods, pharmacy sourcing and staff opt-out policies. Most providers have no playbook, so patients bounce between systems that opt out. Advocacy groups cover navigation, not staffing.
solution: A turnkey program: policy templates, staff training, state-specific e-documentation workflows, an on-call roster of trained consulting physicians and evaluators (licensed per state, telehealth where allowed), pharmacy coordination, family support, and post-death reporting. The service serves only patient-initiated requests and supports providers that opt in.
why_now: New York's law was signed Feb 6, 2026, and Illinois's law, signed Dec 12, 2025, takes effect this month (Sept 2026). Two large states are opening within months, with 14 jurisdictions now having some form of law and more pending. Scheduled deaths also create planning lead time that sudden deaths never had.
revenue_model: $15-40K program onboarding fee, $500-$1,000 per consult or evaluation, and per-case coordination fees. State grants are possible.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce input is not legal permission but willing clinicians and paperwork bandwidth, so the money is in clinical capacity and compliance, which advocacy nonprofits don't provide.
first_30_days: Sign 2-3 physicians with prior Oregon or Washington experience as advisors. Approach 10 independent Illinois hospices. Sell a $7.5K readiness assessment plus policy pack first. Start recruiting a consulting-physician roster and get counsel to confirm state rules on telehealth and referral fees.

title: Ex-Botter Red Team for Limited Drops
one_liner: Pay former sneaker-bot users to attack your product drop before launch, then rent you the checkout filter that stops what they found.
customer: Indie brands that run limited drops on Shopify with 500 to 5,000 units: streetwear labels, collectible toy and art-toy makers, TCG shops, sneaker boutiques, merch stores, small beauty and food brands. They pay $750 to $2,500 per pentest, then a per-drop or monthly fee.
problem: Brands think a waiting room or Cloudflare stops scalpers. It only stops speed. Real resellers win by multiplying identities, not by being fast. They use Gmail dot and plus tricks and catch-all domains, address jigging (Apt vs Unit vs #, an extra letter in the street name), virtual cards from one issuer, and residential proxies. One 'customer' becomes 40 orders. Fans get nothing, the brand gets angry DMs, and the resale premium goes to strangers. Small brands cannot afford enterprise bot vendors and do not know what to look for.
solution: Wedge: a 'Drop Pentest'. We run a real reseller stack against the brand's store or staging a week before launch and hand back a report: 'we would have captured 38% of your units, here is how'. Product: a Shopify checkout app called One Per Human. It normalizes emails, fuzzy-dedupes addresses (USPS-style standardization plus apartment and unit variants), clusters card fingerprints and BINs, phone-verifies and blocks VoIP numbers, and flags or auto-cancels suspected multiples before fulfillment, with a human review queue. Optional 'verified reseller tier' at a higher price so the brand captures some of the flip premium legitimately.
why_now: Collectible drops have become a public mess in 2025-26: Labubu and other Pop Mart drops, and Pokemon TCG releases where stores had fights, lines, and pulled product. Indie brands now copy sneaker-style drops, with sneaker-style bot pressure. Cheap LLM fuzzy matching makes address and identity dedupe far cheaper to build than it was two years ago. Shopify's checkout extensibility gives apps a place to validate or flag orders.
revenue_model: Pentest at $750 to $2,500. Guard app at $149 to $499 per drop, or 0.5% to 1% of drop GMV. Annual contracts for brands that drop monthly.
non_obvious_insight: Bots do not beat drops on speed. They beat them on identity multiplication, and the tells sit in the order data (address shape, email pattern, card issuer clusters) that the brand already has. Only someone who has run the tricks knows which tells matter. The poacher-turned-gamekeeper credibility is the moat, and the pentest report sells the product by showing the brand its own leak.
first_30_days: Days 1 to 7: build the attack checklist from what I and my Discord friends already do. Days 7 to 14: DM 100 small Shopify brands with an upcoming drop on Instagram, offering a free mini-audit built from their public store, such as how easy it is to create fake variants of an address. Days 14 to 30: convert 3 to 5 into paid pentests at $750 and use the findings to pre-sell the app. Delivery is mostly a spreadsheet plus screenshots.

title: Cryo-Vault for Artisan Food Microbial Cultures
one_liner: Backup-and-rescue service that fingerprints, isolates and cryo-banks the living house cultures (cheese rind flora, koji, kombucha SCOBYs, sourdough starters, mushroom spawn, natural-wine yeast) of small food producers in split-geography -80 storage, with a 48-hour emergency revival.
customer: Small artisan producers: raw-milk and farmstead cheesemakers, koji, miso and sake makers, kombucha brewers, specialty mushroom growers, sourdough bakeries, natural winemakers and cideries. Pay $250-400 intake plus $20-40/month per culture, and $400-600 per emergency rescue.
problem: A small producer's house culture is their product identity, yet it lives on the counter or in a single fridge, propagated by serial subculture. Mother cultures senesce and drift, contaminate, or get wiped out by phage (dairy) or Trichoderma-type molds (mushrooms). One crash can end a brand for months. Big culture houses won't bank a small producer's strains, and commercial biobank services are priced and designed for pharma.
solution: A mail-in kit: send a gram of culture, get back an ITS/16S-based composition fingerprint, viability and purity report, and isolated key strains. Each is banked as glycerol stocks in triplicate at two separate sites, with a dashboard of banked cultures. The rescue tier revives a viable working culture in 48 hours with contamination diagnosis, and later adds a periodic 'drift check' compared against the banked baseline. Optional fingerprint certificates for craft-authenticity claims and geographic-indication programs.
why_now: Fermentation and koji-based craft food is booming, and sequencing costs are trivial (about $30 per amplicon sample). Consolidation and climate stress are raising the cost of a culture crash. Small food makers increasingly market on 'living' and heritage claims that they can't currently back up. Laid-off microbiologists can staff this cheaply.
revenue_model: Intake fee plus recurring monthly vault subscription per culture. Per-event rescue fees. Fingerprint certificates and drift-check add-ons. Later B2B with food-safety consultants and craft trade associations, which bundle it as a member benefit.
non_obvious_insight: Cryo-banking with a genetic fingerprint is routine bench hygiene for any wet-lab, but the food world has never been offered it at a price small producers can pay. Nobody thinks of 'my sourdough' as a strain to back up until it crashes. The wedge is not the science, it is the packaging as insurance and the rescue promise.
first_30_days: Bank 10 cultures for free from friendly producers (cheesemakers, kombucha and mushroom growers) recruited through guild forums and Facebook groups. Rent -80 space at a university core, a co-lab or a local biobank. Use a commercial amplicon sequencing service for fingerprints. Publish one story about a rescued culture. Convert the first cohort to $99/month founding-member pricing. Stay strictly with BSL-1 food-grade organisms and set clear policies on pathogen refusal and shipping.

title: Demumu With a Body: Paid Welfare-Check Responders
one_liner: Parent-paid check-in safety for Chinese-, Indian- and Korean-speaking students and migrants living alone abroad, where a missed check-in triggers a paid local door-knock instead of an email to someone 10,000 km away.
customer: Parents (in China, India, Korea) of students and young professionals living alone abroad, who pay about $6/month plus about $45 per dispatched welfare check. Universities' international offices are a secondary channel.
problem: The viral Chinese app 'Are You Dead?' (renamed Demumu) proves demand for solo-living safety, but its only action is an email alert to two emergency contacts. For migrants those contacts are usually parents or friends in another city or country who cannot physically check. China has more than 125 million one-person households, projected at 200 million by 2030. About two-thirds of solo dwellers are aged 20-59, i.e. young migrants rather than the elderly.
solution: A student-controlled check-in app (student chooses the circle, parents pay). After a missed check-in, the escalation is: push, SMS and call, then roommates and landlord, and finally a vetted local responder who does a door-knock with a photo-verified report and can escalate to the local non-emergency welfare-check line or emergency services. The responders are recruited from the same student and gig pool as China's 'companion economy' providers, in host cities such as Boston, London, Sydney and Toronto.
why_now: Demumu's rebrand and global launch in January 2026 put the format on top of app charts in China and among paid utilities in the West, so users now trust the idea. Anyone can clone the basic check-in app in a weekend, since it reportedly cost about ¥1,500 to build. The defensible layer is physical response, which the viral app doesn't have. A 50 billion yuan ($7.4B) Chinese 'companionship economy' shows that people pay for on-demand human presence.
revenue_model: $6/month parent subscription, plus $45 per dispatch or prepaid packs of two. Later, university international-office licensing and insurer partnerships (travel and student health plans).
non_obvious_insight: The buyer is not the solo-liver. It is the anxious relative paying $30-60k a year in tuition, for whom $6/month is trivial. The viral product's critical gap is what happens after the alert. Evidence: Demumu reportedly cost about ¥1,500 ($210) to build, alerts two emergency contacts by email, most solo dwellers are 20-59, and there are 125 million one-person households (https://theconversation.com/are-you-dead-chinas-viral-app-reveals-a-complex-reality-of-solo-living-and-changing-social-ties-274536). It was the top paid app in China at 8 yuan and hit the top paid utilities in Australia (https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/1/14/chinese-app-are-you-dead-to-change-name-after-surge-in-popularity and https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-01-15/are-you-dead-app-changes-name-demumu/106228484). Companion providers already earn 3,000-5,000 yuan/month and one hiking firm grew from under 10 to 370 workers (https://finance.yahoo.com/economy/articles/hiking-hotpot-lonely-consumers-china-031456787.html), so a responder supply pool exists.
first_30_days: Days 1-7: White-label a check-in flow (Twilio plus a simple app or LINE/WeChat mini-program) and write parent-facing Chinese copy. Recruit and vet 10 responders (graduate students) in 3 cities, with a code of conduct and background check. Days 8-20: Post on Xiaohongshu 'studying abroad' and 'parents of overseas students' and in WeChat parent groups, offering a free first month. Days 21-30: Convert 100 parent subscribers, run at least 3 real dispatches and publish the anonymized outcomes. Test privacy and consent wording with 20 students, because the student must opt in and control the circle. Assumption to test: parents' willingness to pay, and student acceptance.

title: Finishing Milk Run for Small Machine Shops
one_liner: A scheduled truck route and capacity-slot exchange that pools small lots from many shops into full tank loads and racks at platers, anodizers, heat treaters and powder coaters.
customer: Job shops and small OEM plants (5-150 employees) that machine or fabricate parts but outsource plating, anodize, passivation, heat treat, e-coat or powder coat. The buyer is the shop owner or plant manager. The second customer is the finisher, who gets fuller tanks and lines.
problem: Everyone talks about a shortage of machinists, but the real reshoring bottleneck is finishing. Parts wait 9-15 days for a truck and for enough volume to fill a tank or rack. Finishers apply minimum-charge lots that punish small runs. Shops drive parts themselves or pay LTL rates of $150-$300 per pallet, and a batch's lead time is mostly waiting, not processing. The 2026 Reshoring Initiative data show finishing capacity as part of the bottleneck, and permits make new capacity slow and rare.
solution: Run daily box-truck routes around a dense corridor (Akron-Canton-Cleveland-Youngstown) with QR-coded totes and text-message status. Pre-buy weekly capacity slots at 8-12 vetted finishers, pool many shops' small lots into shared racks, and guarantee 3-5 day door-to-door turnaround. Route data and slot utilisation decide which finisher gets which parts. Expand to a second corridor (Columbus-Dayton-Cincinnati) once route density works.
why_now: Reshoring is adding machined and fabricated volume in the US while environmental permits have made new plating, anodize and coating lines almost impossible to build. Existing finishers are running full but inefficiently. Lightweight route and tote software plus cheap dispatch tools remove the reason this stayed a hand-arranged, phone-call business.
revenue_model: $55-$95 per stop or tote pickup, an 8-12% margin on capacity-slot resale, and a $299/month booking and tracking subscription. Roughly 40 active shops on one corridor gets to $1M ARR. Later, purchase or co-develop a permitted finishing line inside a 'factory condo'.
non_obvious_insight: An anodize or zinc cycle takes hours. Most of the lead time is a batch waiting for a truck and waiting for enough peers to fill a rack. That is a logistics-and-pooling problem hiding inside what everyone treats as a process-capacity problem, and it is solvable without building a single tank.
first_30_days: Lease one box truck or contract a local courier per stop. Interview 15 shops and 4 finishers. Launch one route on Tuesdays and Thursdays with 8 pilot shops at $65 per stop. Get two finishers to guarantee 48-hour processing for pooled lots in exchange for weekly committed volume. Track everything in Airtable with printed QR tags and text updates, and publish on-time-in-full data after 6 weeks.

title: NFC Open-Item Tags for Aircraft Shift Handover
one_liner: Tamper-evident NFC red-tags that record every opened panel, disconnected line and removed component on an aircraft, and block sign-off until each is closed with an as-left photo.
customer: Directors of maintenance, quality and safety managers at regional airlines, Part 145 shops, Part 135 fleets and helicopter EMS operators. Line stations with 3-6 techs per shift are the beachhead.
problem: The most dangerous moments in line maintenance are shift change and interruption. A tech opens a panel, disconnects a connector or leaves a cap loose, gets pulled to an AOG, and hands over verbally or with a sticky note. The 'system' is a paper red tag, a whiteboard and memory. The 2024 737 MAX 9 door-plug investigation put undocumented removal of fasteners in front of every director of maintenance. Digital task cards do not fix this, because the physical state of the aircraft between task steps is not captured anywhere.
solution: Tamper-evident NFC tags that hang on the physical thing that is open. A tech taps the tag with a phone (offline-first, because hangars have dead zones), records what, why and who, and hangs it. At handover, the app shows a manifest of open tags by tail. The aircraft cannot be released in the app until every tag is closed with an as-left photo. Export goes to the work order as PDF or CSV on day one, and to the maintenance system through an API later. Techs get a time-stamped record of exactly what they did and left.
why_now: The 2024 door-plug event made undocumented maintenance a board-level topic. The FAA's 2024 SMS final rule expanded safety-management obligations to more operators, and safety departments are looking for concrete evidence-capture tools. NFC-capable phones are standard and cheap tags are commodity, so the hardware cost is pennies. AI is a minor part of this, which is a feature. It ships without data-science risk.
revenue_model: Per-aircraft subscription ($75-150 per tail per month) plus consumable tags at $0.50-1.50 each, the razor-and-blade model that made lockout-tagout a large industrial category. Enterprise tier with maintenance-system integration and safety analytics.
non_obvious_insight: Maintenance software dies at the tech's hands, because anything that adds keystrokes gets skipped. This replaces a paper red tag with something faster, and it gives the tech a personal alibi for their own certificate if something is questioned years later. The buyer is quality and safety, not IT, so it needs no integration with the maintenance system to start. Underneath the software is a consumables business.
first_30_days: Ask your own director of maintenance to pilot it at your line station, so you can test it during real shift changes. Build a progressive web app with offline storage and buy 2,000 off-the-shelf NFC stickers. Run a free 30-day pilot at two line stations and one Part 145 shop, then measure tags closed with photo, handover time and missed items caught. Convert the pilot to $99 per tail per month plus tags, and use the measured near-misses as the sales collateral for safety managers.

title: Amnesty Desk: Legalizing Unpermitted Backyard Units
one_liner: Fixed-fee 'legalize your existing unit' service that is paid at closing, turning unpermitted ADUs and garage conversions into appraisable, financeable, insurable square footage.
customer: Homeowners (and heirs) with unpermitted ADUs, basement apartments or garage conversions built before the amnesty cutoff, plus listing agents who need the unit legal before it sells.
problem: Huge numbers of homes contain units built without permits. They can't be appraised as living area, financed, insured properly, or sold without discounts and buyer fear. Owners assume legalization means demolition or a full code retrofit, and city permit counters are unfamiliar with the new amnesty rules.
solution: Productized legalization. A paid feasibility scan (measured as-built drawing, life-safety checklist), then a fixed-price package covering plans, permit filing under the amnesty rules, inspection coordination and any minimal safety fixes. Offer a contingent, paid-at-escrow version for listing agents, and an appraiser-ready package that unlocks HELOCs or refinancing once legal.
why_now: California's AB 2533 took effect January 1, 2025. Cities generally must accept applications for eligible pre-2020 unpermitted ADUs and JADUs without retroactive penalties or full code upgrades, unless the unit is unsafe. Regional guidance was still being issued in March 2026. Some estimates say tens of thousands of additional units are now eligible. Local planning staff are still learning the process. More states are loosening ADU rules.
revenue_model: $1,500-2,500 feasibility and as-built fee, then an $8-15K legalization package. Alternatively a contingent fee of roughly 1% of the sale price paid at close for agent-referred listings. Referral fees from lenders and insurers once units are legal.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce asset is city-by-city procedural knowledge, not architecture: how each of the roughly 500 California jurisdictions actually processes amnesty applications. The buyer of the outcome is often the next buyer, lender or insurer, so price and pitch it as a sale-price unlock ('an extra $80-150K of appraised value') rather than a permit fee. A database of how each city behaves is the compounding moat.
first_30_days: Pick 3 adjacent cities in one region (for example Bay Area or LA basin). Partner with a licensed architect or expediter and a measurement scanner. Build a one-page eligibility checker. Reach out to listing agents and to homeowners who have advertised unpermitted units on rental sites. Close the first 5 feasibility scans at $2,000 each and offer the first 2 legalizations at a discount for case studies.
